_meta.note: HyiBody English one-liners (AI draft, pending review). blurb = the sentence in the info card; fact = the "Did you know" note. Figures are the usual popular-science ranges — set reviewed to true once a human has checked them.

skin.blurb: The skin is the body's largest organ: a waterproof wrapper that also handles touch, temperature control and the first line of defence against germs.
skin.fact: Spread flat, an adult's skin covers about 1.5–2 square metres. You shed tens of thousands of dead cells every minute and grow a whole new outer layer roughly every four weeks.

sternocleidomastoid.blurb: A strap of muscle running diagonally down each side of the neck; it turns the head and tips it forward, and it is the most visible muscle in the neck.
sternocleidomastoid.fact: Its name is its road map — from the sternum and clavicle up to the mastoid bump behind the ear. Turn your head and you can feel it stand out.

platysma.blurb: A thin sheet of muscle just under the skin of the front of the neck; it pulls the corners of the mouth down and tightens the neck skin.
platysma.fact: Those vertical cords that appear on your neck when you grimace are the platysma contracting.

trapezius.blurb: A large flat muscle covering the upper back and the back of the neck; it shrugs the shoulders and steadies and rotates the shoulder blade.
trapezius.fact: Left and right together form a four-sided diamond — a trapezium — which is where the name comes from. The sore spot on top of a stiff shoulder is its upper fibres.

deltoid.blurb: The muscle that caps the shoulder joint and lifts the arm forward, out to the side and backward, giving the shoulder its rounded shape.
deltoid.fact: The "upper outer arm" where vaccines are usually given is the deltoid.

pectoralis_major.blurb: The big fan-shaped muscle across the front of the chest; it pulls the arm inward and forward and does the heavy lifting in a push-up or bench press.
pectoralis_major.fact: It fans out from the collarbone, breastbone and rib cartilages onto a single point on the humerus, so different fibres take over as the arm changes angle.

pectoralis_minor.blurb: A smaller muscle hidden under pectoralis major, running from the ribs to the coracoid process of the shoulder blade, pulling it forward and down.
pectoralis_minor.fact: Slouching for years leaves it short and tight — one of the usual suspects behind rounded shoulders.

serratus_anterior.blurb: A muscle wrapped around the side of the rib cage that pushes the shoulder blade forward and holds it flat against the chest wall.
serratus_anterior.fact: Its saw-toothed edge gives it the name "serratus", and because it drives a punch it is nicknamed the boxer's muscle.

intercostal_muscles.blurb: Short muscles filling the gaps between neighbouring ribs; they lift the ribs when you breathe in and lower them when you breathe out.
intercostal_muscles.fact: The strip of meat between the bones on a rack of ribs is exactly this — an animal's intercostal muscle.

diaphragm.blurb: A dome of muscle separating the chest from the abdomen; it is the main engine of breathing.
diaphragm.fact: A hiccup is the diaphragm twitching involuntarily while the vocal cords snap shut — the snap is the sound.

external_oblique.blurb: The outermost flat muscle of the abdominal wall, its fibres running down and inward to twist and side-bend the trunk and shield the organs.
external_oblique.fact: Its fibres run in the direction your hands slide into your front pockets; the two sides must work together to turn the body.

erector_spinae.blurb: A column of muscles running the length of the spine on both sides, holding the body upright and arching it backward.
erector_spinae.fact: The ache in your lower back after a long day of sitting or standing is usually this group tiring out from holding you up.

levator_scapulae.blurb: Runs from the neck vertebrae to the top corner of the shoulder blade, lifting the blade and helping bend the head sideways.
levator_scapulae.fact: The sharpest point of pain in a stiff neck is often exactly where it attaches to the shoulder blade.

splenius_capitis.blurb: A deep muscle at the back of the neck that tilts the head back and turns it toward the same side.
splenius_capitis.fact: It wraps the deeper neck muscles like a bandage, which is why it is named after the Greek word for a splint.

supraspinatus.blurb: Sits above the spine of the shoulder blade and is one of the four rotator cuff muscles; it starts the arm's lift out to the side.
supraspinatus.fact: Its tendon is the one most often injured in the rotator cuff, because it squeezes through a narrow gap under the tip of the shoulder.

infraspinatus.blurb: Covers most of the back of the shoulder blade, turning the arm outward and holding the shoulder joint steady.
infraspinatus.fact: It is the brake on a throw or a spike, which is why it is unusually well developed in ball players.

teres_major.blurb: Runs from the lower corner of the shoulder blade to the humerus, pulling the arm inward and rotating it inward.
teres_major.fact: It works so closely with latissimus dorsi that it is nicknamed "lat's little helper".

biceps_brachii.blurb: The muscle on the front of the upper arm; it bends the elbow and turns the palm face-up.
biceps_brachii.fact: It is the bulge you flex to show off, but the real workhorse of elbow bending is the brachialis underneath it.

triceps_brachii.blurb: Fills the back of the upper arm and straightens the elbow.
triceps_brachii.fact: It has three heads and makes up most of the arm's muscle volume — training it adds more size than training the biceps.

brachialis.blurb: Hidden beneath the biceps, this is the strongest muscle for bending the elbow.
brachialis.fact: It pulls just as hard with the palm up or down, so it does the quiet, unglamorous half of every curl.

brachioradialis.blurb: Runs along the thumb side of the forearm and bends the elbow most powerfully when the thumb points up.
brachioradialis.fact: That is the grip you use to raise a glass, which is why it is sometimes called the beer-drinker's muscle.

flexor_carpi_radialis.blurb: A muscle on the front of the forearm that bends the wrist and pulls the hand toward the thumb side.
flexor_carpi_radialis.fact: Clench your fist and bend your wrist: the most obvious tendon on the thumb side of your wrist is this one.

palmaris_longus.blurb: A slender muscle on the front of the forearm that tightens the fascia of the palm and helps bend the wrist.
palmaris_longus.fact: About one person in ten is born without it, with no loss of grip strength. Touch your thumb to your little finger and flex the wrist — if a cord pops up in the middle of your wrist, you have one.

flexor_digitorum_superficialis.blurb: Sits on the front of the forearm and bends the middle joints of the fingers.
flexor_digitorum_superficialis.fact: In each finger its tendon splits in two so the deeper tendon can pass through the gap, like a tunnel.

extensor_digitorum.blurb: Sits on the back of the forearm and straightens the fingers and the wrist.
extensor_digitorum.fact: The cords that stand out on the back of your hand when you spread your fingers are its tendons, one per finger.

psoas_major.blurb: Runs from the lumbar spine to the thigh bone; it is the main hip flexor that lifts the thigh, and it also steadies the lower back.
psoas_major.fact: Long hours of sitting leave it short and tight, which is why standing up straight can feel stiff at first.

iliacus.blurb: Lines the inner surface of the hip bone and joins psoas major to form the iliopsoas, the pair that lifts the thigh.
iliacus.fact: Every stride you run and every stair you climb depends on it.

gluteus_maximus.blurb: One of the largest and strongest muscles in the body; it extends the hip so we can stand up, climb and run.
gluteus_maximus.fact: Ours is far bigger than any other primate's — anatomists count it as a key part of why humans walk upright and run long distances.

gluteus_medius.blurb: Sits on the upper outer side of the hip, swinging the leg outward and keeping the pelvis level when you stand on one leg.
gluteus_medius.fact: When it is weak the pelvis drops with every step, producing the side-to-side gait doctors call a waddle.

tensor_fasciae_latae.blurb: A small muscle at the upper outer thigh that tightens the iliotibial band, helping to flex the hip and stabilise the knee.
tensor_fasciae_latae.fact: The outer-knee pain runners know as IT band syndrome is linked to this muscle and its band being too tight.

sartorius.blurb: The longest muscle in the body, running diagonally across the front of the thigh to the inner knee; it flexes the hip and knee and rotates the thigh outward.
sartorius.fact: Its name comes from the Latin for tailor, because it produces exactly the cross-legged pose that tailors once worked in.

rectus_femoris.blurb: The front-most of the four quadriceps muscles; it both straightens the knee and flexes the hip.
rectus_femoris.fact: It is the only member of the quadriceps that crosses two joints, the hip as well as the knee.

vastus_muscles.blurb: Vastus lateralis and vastus medialis flank the thigh and, with rectus femoris and vastus intermedius, make up the quadriceps that straighten the knee.
vastus_muscles.fact: The teardrop-shaped bulge just above the inner knee is vastus medialis, and it matters a great deal for keeping the kneecap tracking straight.

adductor_muscles.blurb: The group along the inner thigh that pulls the leg back toward the midline.
adductor_muscles.fact: They are what grips a horse's flanks, which is why they are sometimes called the rider's muscles.

hamstrings.blurb: The three muscles at the back of the thigh; together they bend the knee and extend the hip.
hamstrings.fact: They are the classic sprinting injury, because at top speed they must brake the swinging lower leg and drive the hip at the same time.

gastrocnemius.blurb: Forms the bulge of the calf, pushing off from the toes and helping bend the knee.
gastrocnemius.fact: It has two heads, and the explosive power behind a jump or a sprint start comes mostly from it.

soleus.blurb: Lies beneath gastrocnemius and is shaped like a flatfish; it supplies the steady push that holds you upright.
soleus.fact: By squeezing the calf veins it pushes blood back to the heart, which earns it the nickname "the second heart".

calcaneal_tendon.blurb: Joins the calf muscles to the heel bone and is the thickest, strongest tendon in the body.
calcaneal_tendon.fact: It is also called the Achilles tendon, after the one weak spot of the Greek hero.

tibialis_anterior.blurb: Runs down the front and outer side of the shin, lifting the foot so the toes clear the ground as you walk.
tibialis_anterior.fact: The shin soreness new runners feel is usually this muscle protesting a sudden jump in mileage.

tibialis_posterior.blurb: A deep muscle of the calf that holds up the arch of the foot and turns the sole inward.
tibialis_posterior.fact: When it weakens, the arch gradually collapses — the usual cause of adult-acquired flat foot.

fibularis_longus.blurb: Runs down the outer side of the calf, turning the sole outward and pushing off from the toes.
fibularis_longus.fact: Its tendon hooks behind the outer ankle and crosses the sole of the foot, slinging under the arch like a stirrup.

extensor_digitorum_longus.blurb: Sits on the front and outer shin and straightens the outer four toes while lifting the foot.
extensor_digitorum_longus.fact: Lift your toes and the cords that spring up across the top of your foot are its four tendons.

flexor_digitorum_longus.blurb: A deep muscle at the back of the calf that curls the outer four toes.
flexor_digitorum_longus.fact: It is what grips the ground with your toes and what does the work when you walk barefoot on sand.

skull.blurb: Some twenty bones locked together along zigzag sutures, forming a helmet around the brain and the sense organs.
skull.fact: A baby's skull still has soft gaps called fontanelles, so the head can squeeze through the birth canal and the brain has room to grow.

mandible.blurb: The only movable bone of the skull; it hinges on the temporal bone to chew and to speak.
mandible.fact: It is the largest and strongest bone of the face, and its two jaw joints are among the most heavily used joints in the body.

hyoid.blurb: A small U-shaped bone in the front of the neck, slung between muscles and ligaments, giving the tongue and larynx something to pull against.
hyoid.fact: It is the only bone in the body that forms no joint with any other bone.

cervical_vertebrae.blurb: The seven neck vertebrae support the head and let it turn freely; the vertebral arteries thread up through them.
cervical_vertebrae.fact: Almost every mammal has exactly seven of them, no matter how long the neck — giraffes included.

thoracic_vertebrae.blurb: The twelve chest vertebrae each carry a pair of ribs, and together they build the cage that protects the heart and lungs.
thoracic_vertebrae.fact: Tethered by the ribs, this is the least mobile stretch of the whole spine.

lumbar_vertebrae.blurb: The five lower-back vertebrae are the largest in the spine and carry most of the weight of the upper body.
lumbar_vertebrae.fact: Bending over to lift something can load the lumbar disks with several times your body weight, which is why squatting down is the safer way.

sacrum.blurb: Five sacral vertebrae fused into a triangular wedge between the hip bones, passing the weight of the spine into the pelvis.
sacrum.fact: It is still several separate bones in adolescence and only fuses completely in adulthood.

intervertebral_disks.blurb: Cushions between the vertebrae: a tough fibrous ring around a water-rich core that absorbs shock.
intervertebral_disks.fact: They squash slightly through the day and rebound overnight, so you are about a centimetre taller in the morning than at bedtime.

ribs.blurb: Twelve pairs of curved bones forming a cage around the heart and lungs, rising and falling with every breath.
ribs.fact: The lowest two pairs never reach the sternum, so they are called floating ribs — some people can feel their loose ends at the waist.

costal_cartilages.blurb: Connect the front ends of the ribs to the breastbone, making the chest wall both firm and springy.
costal_cartilages.fact: That springiness is what lets CPR compress the breastbone several centimetres and let it rebound again.

sternum.blurb: The breastbone runs down the front of the chest in three parts — manubrium, body and xiphoid process — anchoring the collarbones and rib cartilages.
sternum.fact: CPR compressions belong on the lower half of the sternum, not on the xiphoid process below it.

clavicle_right.blurb: The collarbone is an S-shaped strut across the base of the neck that props the arm away from the trunk.
clavicle_right.fact: It is one of the most commonly broken bones: the shock of falling onto an outstretched hand travels straight up to it.

clavicle_left.blurb: The collarbone is an S-shaped strut across the base of the neck that props the arm away from the trunk.
clavicle_left.fact: It is the first bone in the body to start turning into bone and the last to finish, not completing the job until the mid-twenties.

scapula_right.blurb: The shoulder blade is a triangular plate riding on the upper back, held mostly by muscle, giving the arm a mobile base.
scapula_right.fact: It has almost no bony attachment to the trunk, which is exactly why it can glide and rotate so far with the arm.

scapula_left.blurb: The shoulder blade is a triangular plate riding on the upper back, held mostly by muscle, giving the arm a mobile base.
scapula_left.fact: The socket of the shoulder joint sits on its outer corner and is very shallow — the reason the shoulder is both the most mobile and the most easily dislocated joint.

humerus_right.blurb: The single long bone of the upper arm, meeting the shoulder blade above and the radius and ulna below.
humerus_right.fact: Banging the inside of your elbow and feeling a jolt to your fingers is the ulnar nerve being squeezed behind a knob of the humerus.

humerus_left.blurb: The single long bone of the upper arm, meeting the shoulder blade above and the radius and ulna below.
humerus_left.fact: Humerus has nothing to do with humour, yet the spot where the nerve gets pinched is known everywhere as the funny bone.

radius_right.blurb: The forearm bone on the thumb side; it pivots around the ulna to turn the palm over.
radius_right.fact: Falling onto an outstretched hand most often breaks the radius at its wrist end.

radius_left.blurb: The forearm bone on the thumb side; it pivots around the ulna to turn the palm over.
radius_left.fact: When you turn your palm from up to down, it is the radius that crosses over the ulna — the ulna barely moves.

ulna_right.blurb: The forearm bone on the little-finger side; its upper end, the olecranon, forms the point of the elbow and a stable hinge with the humerus.
ulna_right.fact: The hard knob you feel at the tip of your elbow is the olecranon of the ulna.

ulna_left.blurb: The forearm bone on the little-finger side; its upper end, the olecranon, forms the point of the elbow and a stable hinge with the humerus.
ulna_left.fact: The name comes from the old practice of measuring cloth by the forearm — an ell was roughly one ulna.

carpal_bones.blurb: Eight small bones in two rows that let the wrist bend, straighten and tilt side to side.
carpal_bones.fact: A wrist that keeps aching after a sprain sometimes hides a scaphoid fracture, which is notoriously hard to see on an early X-ray.

hand_bones.blurb: Five metacarpals and fourteen phalanges, plus the carpals, give each hand 27 bones — the most finely engineered tool in the body.
hand_bones.fact: The two hands hold 54 bones, more than a quarter of the entire skeleton, which is what buys us such delicate movement.

hip_bone_right.blurb: The hip bone is the ilium, ischium and pubis fused into one; the two of them plus the sacrum enclose the pelvis.
hip_bone_right.fact: The sitting bones you rest on are its lower part, and they are exactly what starts to ache on a hard bench.

hip_bone_left.blurb: The hip bone is the ilium, ischium and pubis fused into one; the two of them plus the sacrum enclose the pelvis.
hip_bone_left.fact: In childhood the three bones are joined only by cartilage; they fuse into one at the hip socket after puberty.

femur_right.blurb: The thigh bone is the longest and strongest bone in the body, its head set into the hip socket and its lower end forming the knee.
femur_right.fact: It is roughly a quarter of your height, which is why forensic scientists use it to estimate how tall someone was.

femur_left.blurb: The thigh bone is the longest and strongest bone in the body, its head set into the hip socket and its lower end forming the knee.
femur_left.fact: The femoral neck is one of the most common fracture sites after a fall in old age, and the focus of most fall-prevention advice.

patella_right.blurb: The kneecap is a small triangular bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon; it shields the front of the knee and gives the muscle better leverage.
patella_right.fact: It is the largest sesamoid bone in the body — a bone that grows inside a tendon.

patella_left.blurb: The kneecap is a small triangular bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon; it shields the front of the knee and gives the muscle better leverage.
patella_left.fact: When a doctor taps your knee to test the reflex, the target is the tendon just below the kneecap.

tibia_right.blurb: The thick inner bone of the lower leg, carrying nearly all of its load.
tibia_right.fact: The shin you can feel right under the skin is the tibia; almost no muscle covers its front edge, which is why knocking it hurts so much.

tibia_left.blurb: The thick inner bone of the lower leg, carrying nearly all of its load.
tibia_left.fact: It is the second-longest bone in the body, after the femur.

fibula_right.blurb: The slender outer bone of the lower leg; it carries almost no weight and mainly anchors muscle and forms the outer ankle.
fibula_right.fact: Because it bears so little load, surgeons often harvest a length of it to rebuild bone lost elsewhere.

fibula_left.blurb: The slender outer bone of the lower leg; it carries almost no weight and mainly anchors muscle and forms the outer ankle.
fibula_left.fact: The bump on the outside of your ankle is the lower end of the fibula.

tarsal_bones.blurb: Seven bones forming the back of the foot and the base of the arch; the largest of them is the heel bone.
tarsal_bones.fact: The heel bone takes the full shock of landing, which is why it is the bone most often injured in a fall from a height.

foot_bones.blurb: Five metatarsals and fourteen phalanges join the tarsal bones to give each foot 26 bones.
foot_bones.fact: The toe bones are laid out almost exactly like the finger bones, only shorter and thicker — built for bearing weight rather than gripping.

heart.blurb: A fist-sized muscular pump with two atria and two ventricles, driving blood to the lungs and around the body without pause.
heart.fact: It beats about 100,000 times a day and some 2.5–3 billion times in a lifetime, moving enough blood to fill dozens of swimming pools.

lung_right.blurb: The right lung has three lobes, is slightly larger than the left, and is where most gas exchange happens.
lung_right.fact: The two lungs hold hundreds of millions of air sacs; unfolded, their surface would cover about 70 square metres — half a tennis court.

lung_left.blurb: The left lung has only two lobes and is a little smaller than the right, because it has to make room for the heart.
lung_left.fact: Lungs contain no muscle of their own. The diaphragm and rib muscles change the volume of the chest and the air simply follows.

trachea.blurb: The windpipe runs about 10–12 cm from the larynx to the bronchi, held open by a stack of C-shaped cartilage rings.
trachea.fact: The gap in each ring faces backward toward the oesophagus, leaving it room to bulge when you swallow something large.

esophagus.blurb: A muscular tube about 25 cm long that pushes food from the throat to the stomach by waves of contraction.
esophagus.fact: Because it works by muscle rather than gravity, you can swallow perfectly well standing on your head.

stomach.blurb: The widened mixing vessel of the gut, where acid and enzymes break food down into a paste.
stomach.fact: Stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve metal; the lining survives by secreting mucus constantly and replacing itself every few days.

liver.blurb: The largest internal organ, running hundreds of jobs at once: processing nutrients, detoxifying, building proteins and making bile.
liver.fact: It regenerates remarkably well — after most of it is removed it can grow back to near its original size within months.

gallbladder.blurb: A small pear-shaped sac tucked under the liver that stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the small intestine to digest fat.
gallbladder.fact: Bile is concentrated several times over inside it, and when the mix goes out of balance the surplus can crystallise into gallstones.

pancreas.blurb: Lies across the back of the stomach, secreting digestive enzymes into the gut and hormones such as insulin into the blood to control blood sugar.
pancreas.fact: It is a rare double-duty organ, exocrine and endocrine at once, and the hormone-making islets are only a tiny fraction of its bulk.

spleen.blurb: Sits in the upper left abdomen, filtering worn-out red blood cells and taking part in immune defence.
spleen.fact: It is not essential — people live normally after it is removed following injury, though their risk of certain infections is a little higher.

kidneys.blurb: A pair of filters beside the spine at waist level; they clean the blood, make urine and regulate salt, water and blood pressure.
kidneys.fact: Together they filter about 180 litres a day and pass only 1–2 litres as urine — nearly everything else is reabsorbed.

urinary_bladder.blurb: A stretchy reservoir in the pelvis that swells as it fills with urine and squeezes down to empty it.
urinary_bladder.fact: The urge usually starts at around 150–200 ml, and a comfortable full bladder holds roughly 400–500 ml.

small_intestine.blurb: Coiled through the middle of the abdomen and 5–7 metres long, this is where most digestion and nutrient absorption happens.
small_intestine.fact: Villi and microvilli multiply its inner surface to about 30 square metres — roughly the floor of a small room.

large_intestine.blurb: Frames the small intestine, runs about 1.5 metres, and mainly reclaims water and forms stool.
large_intestine.fact: It houses tens of trillions of bacteria, about as many cells as the body's own, helping with digestion and immunity.

tongue.blurb: A bundle of agile muscle that moves food around, senses taste and shapes almost every sound we speak.
tongue.fact: The famous "tongue map" of sweet at the tip and bitter at the back is a long-lived myth — every taste can be sensed all over the tongue.

appendix.blurb: A narrow blind-ended tube hanging off the caecum in the lower right abdomen.
appendix.fact: Long dismissed as useless, it is now thought to act as a safe house for helpful gut bacteria and to carry immune tissue.

adrenal_glands.blurb: Perched like caps on top of each kidney, they release stress hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol.
adrenal_glands.fact: The racing heart and sweaty palms of a fright are adrenaline taking effect within seconds.

ureters.blurb: Two narrow tubes about 25–30 cm long that squeeze urine from the kidneys down to the bladder.
ureters.fact: A kidney stone stuck in a ureter causes what is often ranked among the most severe pains people ever experience.

pituitary_gland.blurb: No bigger than a pea and tucked into a hollow at the base of the skull, it directs the thyroid, adrenals, gonads and much of the endocrine system.
pituitary_gland.fact: The growth hormone it releases decides how tall we grow, which is why it is called the master gland.

larynx_cartilages.blurb: The cartilages that frame the voice box; the largest is the thyroid cartilage, whose front ridge forms the Adam's apple.
larynx_cartilages.fact: In male puberty these cartilages enlarge and the vocal cords lengthen, so the Adam's apple juts out and the voice drops.

thymus.blurb: Sits behind the breastbone and is the school where T lymphocytes mature.
thymus.fact: It is at its largest in childhood, shrinks after puberty and is mostly replaced by fat in adults.

prostate.blurb: A chestnut-sized gland in the male pelvis wrapped around the urethra; it contributes part of the seminal fluid.
prostate.fact: It grows with age and squeezes the urethra running through it, which is why urine flow often slows in older men.

testes.blurb: Held in the scrotum, they produce sperm and secrete the male hormone testosterone.
testes.fact: They sit outside the body because sperm production needs a temperature 2–3 °C below the body's core.

heart_ventricle_wall.blurb: The thickest muscle of the heart; when it contracts it drives blood to the lungs and around the body.
heart_ventricle_wall.fact: The left ventricle wall is about a centimetre thick, three times the right — it has to reach the whole body, while the right only reaches the lungs.

heart_atrium_wall_left.blurb: The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood returning through the pulmonary veins and hands it on to the left ventricle.
heart_atrium_wall_left.fact: Four openings sit in its back wall — the mouths of the four pulmonary veins.

heart_atrium_wall_right.blurb: The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the two venae cavae and hands it on to the right ventricle.
heart_atrium_wall_right.fact: The heart's natural pacemaker, the sinoatrial node, is buried in its wall near where the superior vena cava enters.

heart_mitral_valve.blurb: Sits between the left atrium and left ventricle, its two leaflets stopping blood from washing back into the atrium.
heart_mitral_valve.fact: It is named for its likeness to a bishop's mitre.

heart_tricuspid_valve.blurb: Sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, its three leaflets blocking backflow.
heart_tricuspid_valve.fact: The leaflets are tethered to the papillary muscles by chordae tendineae, like parachute lines, so blood pressure cannot flip them inside out.

heart_aortic_valve.blurb: Guards the outlet of the left ventricle; three half-moon cusps keep blood from falling back out of the aorta.
heart_aortic_valve.fact: The shorter, sharper second heart sound is this valve closing together with the pulmonary valve.

heart_pulmonary_valve.blurb: Guards the outlet of the right ventricle, releasing blood toward the lungs and stopping it from returning.
heart_pulmonary_valve.fact: Its three cusps work like little pockets: blood trying to flow back fills them and snaps the valve shut.

heart_papillary_muscles.blurb: Cone-shaped muscular pillars on the inner wall of the ventricles that hold the valve leaflets through the chordae tendineae.
heart_papillary_muscles.fact: They tighten the cords just before the ventricle squeezes, so the high-pressure blood cannot push the leaflets up into the atrium.

aorta.blurb: The body's widest artery: it leaves the left ventricle, arches over and runs down the trunk, distributing oxygen-rich blood everywhere.
aorta.fact: It is about 2.5–3 cm across where it starts, and the force of each heartbeat makes it visibly pulse.

pulmonary_trunk.blurb: Leaves the right ventricle and quickly divides into the left and right pulmonary arteries, carrying oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
pulmonary_trunk.fact: It is one of the few arteries carrying oxygen-poor blood — artery and vein are defined by direction of flow, not by oxygen content.

pulmonary_arteries.blurb: The left and right pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle into the lungs, where gas exchange takes place.
pulmonary_arteries.fact: Pressure in the lung circuit is only about a sixth of that in the body circuit, which is why the right ventricle is so much thinner than the left.

pulmonary_veins.blurb: Four veins returning freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
pulmonary_veins.fact: They are the only veins in the body that carry oxygen-rich blood.

coronary_arteries.blurb: Branch off the root of the aorta and wrap around the surface of the heart to feed the heart muscle itself.
coronary_arteries.fact: They sit on the heart like a crown, which is what coronary means; when one blocks, the starved muscle dies — a heart attack.

superior_vena_cava.blurb: Collects blood returning from the head, neck and arms and empties it into the right atrium.
superior_vena_cava.fact: It has no valves; the return depends on the suction created inside the chest each time you breathe in.

inferior_vena_cava.blurb: The widest vein in the body, gathering blood from the lower body and abdominal organs and returning it to the right atrium.
inferior_vena_cava.fact: It runs up tight against the right of the spine, where a late-pregnancy uterus can press on it — hence the advice to sleep on your side.

common_carotid_arteries.blurb: Run up either side of the neck and split at the level of the Adam's apple into internal and external carotid arteries feeding the head and neck.
common_carotid_arteries.fact: The strong pulse you find by pressing beside the Adam's apple is this artery.

internal_carotid_arteries.blurb: Pass through the base of the skull into the cranial cavity and are the main supply to the front of the brain and to the eye.
internal_carotid_arteries.fact: Inside the skull it makes several tight turns in an S shape that radiologists call the carotid siphon.

internal_jugular_veins.blurb: Run alongside the internal carotid arteries and form the main return route for blood from the head and neck.
internal_jugular_veins.fact: It is one of the routes doctors most often choose when placing a central venous line.

vertebral_arteries.blurb: Branch from the subclavian arteries, thread up through holes in the neck vertebrae and enter the skull to supply the brainstem and cerebellum.
vertebral_arteries.fact: They are strung through the vertebrae like beads on a thread, so neck problems can occasionally affect blood flow to the back of the brain.

brachiocephalic_trunk.blurb: The first branch off the aortic arch; it soon divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.
brachiocephalic_trunk.fact: Only the right side has one — on the left the carotid and subclavian arteries come straight off the arch.

brachiocephalic_veins.blurb: Each is formed where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet, and the two of them join to make the superior vena cava.
brachiocephalic_veins.fact: The left one is far longer than the right, because it has to cross the midline of the body to reach its partner.

subclavian_arteries.blurb: Pass beneath the collarbone as the main blood supply to the arm, and also give off the vertebral arteries to the brain.
subclavian_arteries.fact: It presses a shallow groove into the first rib — a mark of just how tightly vessel and bone are packed together here.

subclavian_veins.blurb: Carry blood from the arm back into the chest and join the internal jugular veins to form the brachiocephalic veins.
subclavian_veins.fact: This is where the body's lymph finally drains back into the bloodstream, at the venous angle nearby.

axillary_brachial_arteries.blurb: The axillary artery crosses the armpit and continues as the brachial artery down the inner upper arm, supplying the whole limb.
axillary_brachial_arteries.fact: When your blood pressure is taken, the stethoscope is listening to flow in the brachial artery.

forearm_arteries.blurb: The radial and ulnar arteries split from the brachial artery at the elbow and run down the thumb and little-finger sides of the forearm into the hand.
forearm_arteries.fact: The pulse you count at the wrist is the radial artery; the two arteries link into arches in the palm, so one can cover if the other is blocked.

celiac_trunk.blurb: The first big branch of the abdominal aorta — very short, and immediately dividing into the arteries of the stomach, liver and spleen.
celiac_trunk.fact: It is only a centimetre or two long yet supplies most of the organs of the upper abdomen.

mesenteric_arteries.blurb: The superior and inferior mesenteric arteries leave the abdominal aorta and run through the mesentery to feed the small and large intestine.
mesenteric_arteries.fact: Blood flow to the gut rises sharply after a meal, one reason hard exercise straight after eating feels so unpleasant.

celiac_branches.blurb: The common hepatic and splenic arteries are the two main branches of the celiac trunk, supplying the liver, gallbladder and stomach, and the spleen.
celiac_branches.fact: The splenic artery winds along the top edge of the pancreas and is one of the most tortuous arteries in the abdomen.

portal_tributaries.blurb: The splenic and mesenteric veins collect blood from the spleen, stomach and intestines and merge to form the hepatic portal vein.
portal_tributaries.fact: Everything absorbed by the gut — nutrients and swallowed medicines alike — travels this way to the liver for screening first.

hepatic_portal_vein.blurb: Delivers nutrient-laden blood from the digestive tract into the liver for processing before it joins the general circulation.
hepatic_portal_vein.fact: That gives the liver a double blood supply: nutrients through the portal vein, oxygen through the hepatic artery.

renal_arteries.blurb: Branch off either side of the abdominal aorta and deliver a large share of the blood supply to the kidneys for filtering.
renal_arteries.fact: About a fifth of every heartbeat's output goes to the kidneys, even though together they are under 1% of body weight.

renal_veins.blurb: Return the filtered blood from the kidneys to the inferior vena cava.
renal_veins.fact: The left renal vein has to cross in front of the aorta to get there, so it is noticeably longer than the right.

iliac_arteries.blurb: The abdominal aorta splits in the lower back into the common iliac arteries, each dividing again into an internal branch for the pelvis and an external branch for the leg.
iliac_arteries.fact: The split sits roughly at navel level, in front of the fourth lumbar vertebra.

femoral_arteries.blurb: The main artery of the thigh, entering at the middle of the groin and supplying the whole lower limb.
femoral_arteries.fact: Its pulse is easy to feel in the groin, which is why cardiac catheters are often threaded in from exactly this spot.

femoral_veins.blurb: Run beside the femoral arteries as the main deep drainage route of the leg.
femoral_veins.fact: Sitting still on a long flight lets clots form in these deep veins; getting up and working the calf muscles is what pumps the blood along.

popliteal_arteries.blurb: The continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee, supplying the knee joint and the lower leg.
popliteal_arteries.fact: It lies deep in the hollow behind the knee and is one of the hardest large arteries to find a pulse in.

tibial_arteries.blurb: The anterior and posterior tibial arteries branch from the popliteal artery and run down the front and back of the calf to supply the leg and foot.
tibial_arteries.fact: The pulse you can feel on the top of the foot is the continuation of the anterior tibial artery, a quick check of circulation in the leg.

great_saphenous_veins.blurb: The longest vein in the body, running from the inner side of the foot all the way up to the groin to join the femoral vein.
great_saphenous_veins.fact: The cords that stand out on the calf are usually its branches, and surgeons often harvest it to use as a graft in heart bypass surgery.

azygos_vein.blurb: Runs up the right side of the spine, collecting blood from the chest wall and part of the abdominal wall into the superior vena cava.
azygos_vein.fact: It works as a spare route linking the two venae cavae, taking over the load if the inferior vena cava is obstructed.

brain.blurb: The headquarters of the nervous system, weighing about 1.3–1.4 kg and running thought, sensation, movement and the basics of staying alive.
brain.fact: It is only about 2% of body weight but burns roughly 20% of the body's energy.

spinal_cord.blurb: Housed in the spinal canal, it is the information highway between brain and body, and it handles some reflexes entirely on its own.
spinal_cord.fact: It is much shorter than the spine: in adults it ends around the first or second lumbar vertebra, below which only a bundle of nerve roots — the cauda equina — continues.

optic_nerves.blurb: Carry the light signals picked up by the retina toward the brain — the data cable of vision.
optic_nerves.fact: Each holds over a million nerve fibres, and where it leaves the eye there are no light receptors at all, which creates the blind spot in your field of view.
